Sage will create $LU$ factorizations; once we have a matrix A, we write P, L, U = A.LU() to obtain the matrices $P$, $L$, and $U$ such that $PA = LU$.

In [example-LU], we found the $LU$ factorization $$ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \amp -3 \amp 1 \\ -4 \amp 5 \amp 0 \\ 2 \amp -2 \amp 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ -2 \amp 1 \amp 0 \\ 1 \amp -1 \amp 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \amp -3 \amp 1 \\ 0 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 3 \end{bmatrix}=LU. $$ Using Sage, define the matrix $A$, and then ask Sage for the $LU$ factorization. What are the matrices $P$, $L$, and $U$?

Notice that Sage finds a different $LU$ factorization than we found in the previous example because Sage uses partial pivoting, as described in the previous section, when it performs Gaussian elimination.

Define the vector $\bvec = \threevec8{-13}{8}$ in Sage and compute $P\bvec$.

Use the matrices L and U to solve $L\cvec = P\bvec$ and $U\xvec = \cvec$. You should find the same solution $\xvec$ that we found in the previous example.

Use the factorization to solve the equation $A\xvec = \threevec9{-16}{10}$.

How does the factorization show us that $A$ is invertible and that, therefore, every equation $A\xvec=\bvec$ has a unique solution?

Suppose that we have the matrix $$ B = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 3 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ 2 \amp -1 \amp 1 \\ 2 \amp 1 \amp 3 \\ \end{array}\right] $$ . Use Sage to find the $LU$ factorization. Explain how the factorization shows that $B$ is not invertible.

Consider the matrix $$ C = \left[\begin{array}{rrrr} -2 \amp 1 \amp 2 \amp -1 \\ 1 \amp -1 \amp 0 \amp 2 \\ 3 \amp 2 \amp -1 \amp 0 \\ \end{array}\right] $$ and find its $LU$ factorization. Explain why $C$ and $U$ have the same null space and use this observation to find a basis for $\nul(A)$.
